You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

A demonstration established the rule: input color 4 formed full columns 0, 8, 12 and full rows 5, 6, 10, 17; output recolored every cell of those full lines to color 2, while preserving all other cells exactly (including isolated/noisy 4s). When the grid contains full, uninterrupted uniform horizontal and/or vertical lines that serve as separators, recolor those complete line cells to 2 and leave every other cell unchanged. This directly confirms replication also applies when the partition has three panel rows and two columns.
arc_grid_panel_pattern_replication_across_separators ARC grid-panel pattern replication across separators For ARC puzzles with a grid partitioned into equal-sized panels by full uniform separator rows/columns, a colored pattern in one panel may be the template to copy into every panel. In the demonstrated task, the source was the upper-right panel; copy every cell (including background) at identical within-panel offsets into all other panels, preserving the separator lines and dimensions. Example: 9x17 grid split by color-9 central row/column into four 4x8 panels; the upper-right panel's pattern was repeated in all four panels in the output. A 13x29 test split into six 6x9 panels by color-6 separators used the top-right panel copied into all six panels. First inspect which panel contains a non-background pattern and use the demo to confirm source/direction; do not shift or reflect the template.
arc_separator_grid_cells_with_exactly_two_markers ARC separator-grid panels: mark counts of two or more For ARC inputs partitioned by full uniform horizontal/vertical separator lines into panels, count non-background, non-separator marker cells. Output a grid with one cell per panel: write 1 when count >=2; otherwise use the original background color. Do not assume exactly two: historical task-353e396d evidence includes a 3-marker panel output as 1, so the rule is a minimum threshold. Examples with only 0/1/2 counts cannot distinguish >=2 from ==2. Count carefully and exclude separator lines.
arc_grid_line_corner_agreement_to_compact_cells ARC grid-line corner agreement to compact cells For ARC inputs that are a regular lattice of broad uniform panels separated by horizontal/vertical uniform lines, colored crossings encode each panel: read values at the lattice intersections, then output one cell per adjacent pair of horizontal and vertical separators. Set output[r,c] to the shared intersection color only when all four corners of that panel have the same color; otherwise use the large panel/background color (not the line color). Infer separator coordinates from the repeating full lines and distinguish the background fill inside panels from line color. Verified demo: intersection matrix rows [3,3],[3,3],[2,2],[2,2], background 8 produced [[3],[8],[2]]. Verified this task: 5x5 crossings reduced to 4x4; equal-corner panels became 9,0,4,8 and mismatches became background 1; output [[9,1,1,1],[1,1,1,0],[4,4,1,1],[1,1,1,8]] was correct. This is a compact corner-agreement rule, not a general rule to copy all intersection values.
